newsitem.title: INDIA: Foreign debt funds slow in hedging Indian risk. [CORRECTED 15:21 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Foreign debt funds slow in hedging Indian risk. [CORRECTED 15:21 GMT]

text.p: Foreign funds continue to tread lightly in the Indian debt market despite the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) decision last week to allow hedging in such investments, fund managers and bankers said on Tuesday.
"We have started investing in India in a small way," said an official at a Hong Kong-based investment firm.
"But India is not an open market -- you need too many approvals -- and we are proceeding very slowly," she said.
The official said her firm had not yet planned to take forward cover on its meagre investment in Indian debt.

Earlier this month, the capital market regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) said 13 foreign funds had committed to put more than $2.0 billion in Indian debt but investment so far had been a mere $105.2 million.
"The amount invested -- just over $100 million -- is too small for forward cover," said a bank treasurer adding that foreign investors' cost of funds was about 8.0 percent.
"If you add a cost of forward dollar cover of about 5.0 percent, the effective cost works out to 13 percent," he said.
Debt issues of some of India's blue-chip firms have a yield of about 14 percent. "So forward cover does not make sense at the moment," the bank treasurer said.
He said the picture will change if the yield on Indian debt improved or forward dollar premiums fell to lower levels.

Foreign funds have more at stake in Indian stock markets, where their accumulated investments exceed $8.0 billion, none of which is hedged. The RBI has not allowed forward cover for foreign investment in Indian equities.
But an RBI official told Reuters Television over the weekend that allowing forward cover in equities "was a matter of time."
Foreign funds are more likely to seek forward cover on their equity portfolio, fund managers said.
"In equities, the annualised yield can be as high as 25 or 30 percent, allowing you to hedge currency risk even at high premiums," said a fund manager.
"We have not seen the circular yet," said an official at a foreign bank, referring to the RBI's announcement allowing forward cover to foreign debt funds.
"If you cover one year forward and cancel after six months, what happens?," the official asked. "And if you make money, what are the tax implications?."
Fund managers said the single largest deterrent in investing in Indian debt was the withholding tax of about 20 percent.
"You don't have such high taxation in other countries," said the Indian representative of a foreign fund manager.
